lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach the project Typha pool through rhizomatous marsh habit and the vertically separated staminate-above/pistillate-below spike, then use the gap, leaf width, gland pattern and spike color cautiously for T. domingensis vs T. latifolia.

project_scope.selection_mode: Project module centered on Typha domingensis and Typha latifolia
project_scope.note: Modern Typhaceae contains two accepted genera, Typha and Sparganium, but the current project pool contains only Typha. Species-level Typha calls can be complicated by plasticity and hybridization.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with the inflorescence. In Typha, the upper portion is staminate and the lower dense cylindrical portion is pistillate. Then confirm tall linear leaves arising from a rhizomatous wetland clone.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Robust emergent wetland herbs spreading by rhizomes; leaves long, linear, sheathing at the base and often forming dense clonal stands.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers minute and unisexual, packed into dense cylindrical spikes. In Typha the staminate zone is above the pistillate zone on the same flowering shoot; a naked gap may or may not separate them depending on species and plant.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Each pistillate flower matures a tiny one-seeded fruit associated with long hairs; mature spikes eventually break apart into masses of wind-dispersed fluff.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: For family recognition, ignore the brown 'cigar' stereotype and read the whole flowering spike vertically: male above, female below.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: rhizomatous marsh stand → male-above/female-below spike → flower-to-fluff sequence → T. domingensis vs T. latifolia → grass/sedge/rush comparison
visual_lesson.intro: Cattail ID gets much better when the brown cylinder stops being 'the flower.' It is the female portion of an inflorescence; the male flowers occupy the narrower upper spike and disappear after pollen is shed.

steps.title: 1 · Read the cattail spike vertically
steps.look_for: Upper staminate spike and lower pistillate spike on the same axis.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the core Typha reproductive architecture and the easiest family door in the project.

steps.title: 2 · Follow male spike through anthesis
steps.look_for: The upper staminate section becomes pollen-bearing and later withers or disappears, leaving the persistent female spike below.
steps.why_it_matters: Explains why mature cattails often seem to have only one brown cylinder.

steps.title: 3 · Follow female spike to wind-dispersed fluff
steps.photo_role: pistillate flower → mature brown spike → disintegrating seed fluff
steps.look_for: Dense female flowers form the familiar cylinder, then mature into a mass of tiny fruits with long dispersal hairs.
steps.why_it_matters: Connects flower architecture to the winter seed stage.

steps.title: 4 · Southern cattail door
steps.photo_role: Typha domingensis whole inflorescence + sheath macro
steps.look_for: Male and female spikes usually separated by a visible naked gap; leaves generally narrower; mature female spike often cinnamon to orange-brown. Brown/orange mucilage glands occur on the sheath and proximal blade.
steps.why_it_matters: These are useful field clues for the locally important southern cattail.

steps.title: 5 · Broadleaf cattail door
steps.photo_role: Typha latifolia whole inflorescence + broad leaf
steps.look_for: Male and female spikes usually contiguous or nearly so; leaves generally broader and often glaucous; pistillate bracteoles absent.
steps.why_it_matters: Provides the primary project contrast with T. domingensis.

steps.title: 6 · Know when to stop at Typha
steps.look_for: Intermediate gap, leaf width or spike characters can occur; damaged or poorly developed spikes can mislead.
steps.why_it_matters: FNA warns that detailed flower/bracteole characters and sometimes microscopy are needed for confident species/hybrid calls.

comparisons.title: Typhaceae vs Poaceae
comparisons.rule: Typha has broad linear marsh leaves and dense unisexual spikes, not grass spikelets with glumes, lemma and palea or obvious jointed culm nodes.

comparisons.title: Typhaceae vs Cyperaceae
comparisons.rule: Cattail's massive cylindrical male/female inflorescence is unlike sedge spikelets and one-seeded nutlets. Both can dominate wetlands, so reproductive architecture is the safer family split.

comparisons.title: Typhaceae vs Juncaceae
comparisons.rule: Rushes have small visible 6-tepal flowers and capsules; Typha has minute unisexual flowers packed into dense cylindrical spikes.

comparisons.title: Typha domingensis vs T. latifolia
comparisons.rule: T. domingensis commonly shows a 1–8 cm naked gap, narrower leaves and brown/orange mucilage glands extending onto the proximal blade; T. latifolia commonly has contiguous spikes and broader leaves. Treat these as a character suite, not single-character proof.

visual_lesson.caveat: Typha species hybridize and respond plastically to environment. Gap width and leaf width are useful first-pass characters but are not infallible; technical species confirmation may require bracteole, stigma, gland and pollen characters.
